Ex- The passage states that in Lalu, the two poles of nature, living outside himself and being self-exiled due to the world's hindrances, were always quarreling.
Q13: What is Lalu's involvement in politics after returning to India?
A) He becomes a freedom fighter
B) He joins a political party
C) He engages in political action
D) He stays away from politics
Answer: C
Ex- The passage states that back in India, Lalu is involved in the politics of the twenties and engages in political action.
Q14: Which of Anand's novels is The Big Heart compared to in terms of intensity and concentration?
A) Untouchable
B) Coolie
C) Two Leaves and a Bud
D) The Sword and the Sickle
Answer: A
Ex- The Big Heart is said to reproduce the terrific intensity and concentration of Untouchable.
Q15: Who is Ananta in The Big Heart?
A) A factory owner
B) A coppersmith
C) A freedom fighter
D) A capitalist
Answer: C
Ex- Ananta is described as a man with a 'big heart' who returns from Bombay after participating in the Gandhian struggle for freedom.
Q16: What is Ananta's stance on machines?
A) He opposes them
B) He is indifferent to them
C) He has full faith in them
D) He wants to destroy them
Answer: C
Ex- Ananta has full faith in the machine and sings a refrain about mastering the machine age.
Q17: Who is Janki in The Big Heart?
A) Ananta's wife
B) Ananta's sister
C) Ananta's mistress
D) Ananta's colleague
Answer: C
Ex- Janki is described as Ananta's 'keep' (mistress) who is suffering from tuberculosis.
Q18: What is the time span of events in The Big Heart?
A) A week
B) A month
C) A single day
D) A year
Answer: C
Ex- The novel chronicles the events of a single day, with the tempo increasing hour by hour.
Q19: Who is Ralia in The Big Heart?
A) A factory owner
B) A coppersmith
C) A machine operator
D) A worker
Answer: D
Ex- Ralia is described as one of the workers who is possessed by a sudden frenzy and starts smashing machines in the factory.
Q20: What is the significance of the epigraph in The Big Heart?
A) It is from a speech on the Luddites
B) It is from a play by Hauptmann
C) It is from a novel by Toller
D) It is from a poem by Byron
Answer: A
Ex- The epigraph in The Big Heart is taken from Byron's speech on the Luddites (Nottinghamshire weavers) in the House of Lords.
Q21: What is the name of Victor's mistress in Private Life of an Indian Prince?
A) Janki
B) Gangi
C) Lalla
D) Shampur
Answer: B
Ex- Victor's mistress, who tyrannizes over him, is named Gangi.
Q22: Who makes Victor sign the Instrument of Accession?
A) Sardar Patel
B) Jawaharlal Nehru
C) Mahatma Gandhi
D) Lord Mountbatten
Answer: A
Ex- Sardar Patel summons Victor to Delhi and makes him sign the Instrument of Accession.
Q23: Where does Victor go on an enforced holiday?
A) United States
B) France
C) United Kingdom
D) Russia
Answer: C
Ex- Victor goes to the United Kingdom on an enforced holiday after the administration of Shampur continues to be rotten.
Q24: What happens to Victor at the end of the novel?
A) He is assassinated
B) He abdicates the throne
C) He becomes mad and enters an asylum
D) He goes into exile
Answer: C
Ex- At the end of the novel, Victor opportunely becomes mad and enters an asylum.
Q25: What is the relationship between Victor and Gangi compared to?
A) Prisoners of war
B) Soulmates
C) Master and slave
D) Chameleons
Answer: D
Ex- The relationship between Victor and Gangi is described as a fatal infatuation, like the call of one chameleon for another.
Q26: Which of Anand's later novels reveals more of his humanity and compassion?
A) The Old Woman and the Cow
B) The Road
C) Seven Summers
D) Both A and B
Answer: D
Ex- The passage states that in the later novels, The Old Woman and the Cow (1960) and The Road (1961), Anand reveals more of his humanity and compassion.
Q27: What was the original size of Anand's autobiographical novel written in 1926?
A) 1000 pages
B) 1500 pages
C) 2000 pages
D) 2500 pages
Answer: C
Ex- Anand wrote a 2000-page autobiographical novel in 1926, which he calls "a long confession".
Q28: Why did English publishers not take interest in Anand's autobiographical novel?
A) It was too controversial
B) It was too political
C) It was too huge and amorphous
D) It was too personal
Answer: C
Ex- The autobiographical novel was too huge and too amorphous for English publishers to take an interest in it.
Q29: What is the first part of Anand's autobiographical series called?
A) The Village
B) The Confession
C) Seven Ages
D) Seven Summers
Answer: D
Ex- Anand published the first part of his autobiographical series as Seven Summers in 1951.
Q30: What is the estimated length of Anand's Seven Ages of Man series in its final shape?
A) 2,500 printed pages
B) 3,000 printed pages
C) 3,500 printed pages
D) 4,000 printed pages
Answer: C
Ex- In its final shape, Seven Ages of Man might conceivably run to 3,500 printed pages.
Q1: What does the title Seven Summers signify?
A) The first seven years of the author's life
B) The first seven years of the hero-narrator's life
C) The seven hottest summers in Punjab
D) The seven most significant summers in Indian history
Answer: B
Ex- Seven Summers covers the first seven years of the hero-narrator's life.
Q2: Where is the setting of Seven Summers?
A) Bengal
B) Maharashtra
C) Punjab
D) Tamil Nadu
Answer: C
Ex- Seven Summers is set in the Punjab of the opening decade of the 20th century.
Q3: What is the name of the hero-narrator in Seven Summers?
A) Bakha
B) Munoo
C) Krishan
D) Anand
Answer: C
Ex- The hero-narrator in Seven Summers is named Krishan Chander.
Q4: Who is Krishan Chander partly an incarnation of?
A) Krishna of the Yadus
B) Rama of Ayodhya
C) Shiva of Kailash
D) Vishnu of Vaikuntha
Answer: A
Ex- Krishan Chander is described as partly "an incarnation of Krishna of the Yadus".
Q5: Who tells Krishan the epic stories of 'gods, demons and others'?
A) His father
B) His grandmother
C) His brother
D) His mother
Answer: D
Ex- Krishan's mother tells him the epic stories of 'gods, demons and others'.
Q6: Which childhood friend of Krishan is the original of the character in Untouchable?
A) Munoo
B) Bakha
C) Lachman
D) Dhanoo
Answer: B
Ex- One of Krishan's childhood friends is the sweeper boy, Bakha, evidently the original of the Bakha of Untouchable.
Q7: What event marks the end of Seven Summers?
A) The end of World War I
B) The outbreak of World War I
C) The Indian Independence Movement
D) The Partition of India
Answer: B
Ex- Seven Summers ends with the breaking out of the war in 1914.
Q8: From which Shakespearean play is the title Morning Face derived?
A) Hamlet
B) Macbeth
C) As You Like It
D) Romeo and Juliet
Answer: C
Ex- The title Morning Face is taken from the 'seven ages of man' speech in As You Like It.
Q9: What is the name of Krishan's beloved who is like a second mother to him?
A) Mumtaz
B) Shakuntala
C) Helen
D) Devaki
Answer: D
Ex- Krishan has in his beloved, Devaki, a second mother.
Q10: How many parts does Morning Face consist of?
A) Two
B) Three
C) Four
D) Five
Answer: B
Ex- Morning Face consists of three parts - 'City of Dreadful Nights', 'The Prison' and 'The Regiment'.
Q11: Who is Babu Ram Chand?
A) Krishan's father
B) Krishan's uncle
C) Krishan's teacher
D) Krishan's friend
Answer: A
Ex- Krishan is one of the four sons of Babu Ram Chand.
Q12: Which historical event is portrayed in Morning Face?
A) The Sepoy Mutiny of 1857
B) The Jallianwallah Bagh massacre
C) The Quit India Movement
D) The Partition of India
Answer: B
Ex- The Jallianwallah Bagh atrocity affects Krishan almost directly in Morning Face.
Q13: How many stripes does Krishan receive for disregarding the curfew?
A) Five
B) Six
C) Seven
D) Eight
Answer: C
Ex- Krishan receives seven stripes for disregarding the curfew.
Q14: What is Krishan's ambition?
A) To become a doctor
B) To become a politician
C) To become a poet
D) To become a businessman
Answer: C
Ex- Krishan is determined to find his voice as a poet.
Q15: According to a 'Jewel of Doctors', what are the reasons for Krishan's fret and fever?
A) Tummy upset and crazy brain
B) Canker in the soul and tummy upset
C) Crazy brain and canker in the soul
D) Tummy upset, crazy brain and canker in the soul
Answer: D
Ex- According to a 'Jewel of Doctors', Krishan's fret and fever are due to his 'tummy upset', his 'crazy brain' and to 'a canker in the soul'.
Q16: What does Anand immortalize in 'The Barber's Trade Union'?
A) Bakha the untouchable
B) Munoo the coolie
C) Chanda the barber
D) Gopal the informer
Answer: C
Ex- In 'The Barber's Trade Union', Anand immortalizes Chanda the barber.
Q17: What is the irony in the title of the story 'A Rumour'?
A) There is no rumour in the story
B) The rumour turns out to be true
C) The rumour is about a job, but the protagonist dies
D) The rumour is spread by the protagonist himself
Answer: C
Ex- In 'A Rumour', Dhandu the carpenter goes in search of a job but is run over by a lorry, making the title ironic.
Q18: What happens in 'A Kashmir Idyll'?
A) A Nawab dies of a fit of laughter
B) A Nawab is assassinated
C) A Nawab abdicates his throne
D) A Nawab marries a commoner
Answer: A
Ex- In 'A Kashmir Idyll', a Nawab dies of a fit of laughter.
Q19: What ushers in Ramrajya in 'The Maharaja and the Tortoise'?
A) The Maharaja's wedding
B) The Maharaja's coronation
C) The Maharaja's victory in war
D) The 'crime' in the story
Answer: D
Ex- In 'The Maharaja and the Tortoise', the 'crime' ultimately ushers in Ramrajya.
Q20: What are Anand's notable marks as a writer of fiction?
A) Vitality and keen sense of actuality
B) Psychological depth and ideological complexity
C) Poetic language and symbolic imagery
D) Philosophical musings and introspective characters
Answer: A
Ex- As a writer of fiction, Anand's notable marks are vitality and a keen sense of actuality.
Q21: Who is Anand compared to for describing inequities and idiosyncrasies in the human situation?
A) Leo Tolstoy
B) Fyodor Dostoevsky
C) Charles Dickens
D) Émile Zola
Answer: C
Ex- Anand is described as a veritable Dickens for describing the inequities and idiosyncrasies in the current human situation.
Q22: What do the titles of Anand's early novels seem to emphasize?
A) The particular over the universal
B) The universal over the particular
C) The balance between the universal and the particular
D) The irrelevance of both the universal and the particular
Answer: B
Ex- The titles of Anand's early novels - Untouchable, Coolie, Village - seem to emphasize the universal as against the particular.
Q23: How does Anand make his individual characters assert their uniqueness?
A) By making them rebel against society
B) By giving them lengthy monologues
C) By describing their physical appearance in detail
D) By being a true artist
Answer: D
Ex- Being a true artist, Anand makes the individual character assert his uniqueness without quite ceasing to be the universal.
Q24: What effect does the frequent use of vernacular expressions and swear-words have in Anand's writing?
A) It makes the language poetic
B) It adds psychological depth
C) It sometimes produces a crude or ludicrous effect
D) It creates a philosophical atmosphere
Answer: C
Ex- The frequent use of vernacular expressions and swear-words in Anand's writing often produces a crude or ludicrous effect.
Q25: What does the frequency of vernacular expressions and swear-words do over time in Anand's writing?
A) It makes them sound more offensive
B) It makes them sound empty and almost innocuous
C) It makes them sound more poetic
D) It makes them sound more philosophical
Answer: B
Ex- The very frequency of vernacular expressions and swear-words tends to blunt the edges of their literal meaning, making them sound empty and almost innocuous.
Q26: What carries all before them in Anand's writing despite his undistinguished style?
A) The philosophical depth
B) The poetic language
C) The vitality of his creations and the purposive energy of his narratives
D) The psychological complexity
Answer: C
Ex- Despite Anand often being undistinguished as a writer, the vitality of his creations and the purposive energy of his narratives carry all before them.
Q27: What kind of a writer is Anand described as?
A) A 'committed' writer
B) A 'detached' writer
C) A 'progressive' writer
D) A 'reactionary' writer
Answer: A
Ex- Anand is described as a 'committed' writer.
Q28: With whom does Anand integrate his love for the poor?
A) The intelligentsia
B) The urban middle class
C) The rich and powerful
D) The peasantry
Answer: D
Ex- Anand mentions integrating his love for the poor with actual work for the peasantry.
Q29: Which two figures does Anand mention as choosing the peasantry for their devotion?
A) Marx and Engels
B) Gandhi and Nehru
C) Tolstoy and Gandhi
D) Dickens and Tolstoy
Answer: C
Ex- Anand mentions that both Tolstoy and Gandhi chose the peasantry for their devotion.
Q30: What does Anand feel are the only values given to the intelligentsia in the present time?
A) The creation of art for art's sake
B) The pursuit of wealth and power
C) The alleviation of pain and its expiation
D) The maintenance of the status quo
Answer: C
Ex- Anand feels that the alleviation of pain and its expiation are the only values given to the intelligentsia in the present time.

mcqs.question: Mulk Raj Anand and R. K. Narayan are known for their:
options: Consistency of purpose in writing novels
Expertise in journalism and civil service
Occasional novels as byproducts of other activities
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Anand and Narayan have shown stamina and consistency in their novelistic pursuits, unlike other Indo-Anglian writers.

mcqs.question: Mulk Raj Anand and R. K. Narayan represent:
options: The East and West of India
The North and South of India
The urban and rural divide of India
The pre and post-independence eras of India
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Anand hails from India's North-Western frontier, while Narayan is from the Southern end of the peninsula.

mcqs.question: Mulk Raj Anand's father was originally a:
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Anand's father was a traditional coppersmith who later turned to the army for a living.

mcqs.question: Mulk Raj Anand's mother came from:
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Anand's mother came from a sturdy peasant background.

mcqs.question: The traditional Indian coppersmith's profession demanded:
options: Brain and an eye for beauty
Brawn, brain, patience, and an eye for beauty wedded to utility
mcqs.explanation: Ex- The coppersmith's profession required a combination of physical strength, intelligence, patience, and aesthetic sense.

mcqs.question: With the advance of modern science and technology, traditional village craftsmen:
options: Migrated to cities for regular employment
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Traditional craftsmen lost their occupations and were forced to migrate to cities for employment.

mcqs.question: Mulk Raj Anand derived his compassion for the downtrodden from:
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Anand's understanding of the plight of the poor likely stemmed from his mother's peasant roots.

mcqs.question: Mulk Raj Anand was born in:
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Anand was born in 1905 at Peshawar.

mcqs.question: Mulk Raj Anand's early books included all of the following EXCEPT:
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Anand's early books were "Curries and Other Indian Dishes", "Persian Painting", "The Hindu View of Art", and "The Golden Breath" (not "The Silver Breath").

mcqs.question: The nineteen thirties in India were marked by:
options: The seed-time of modern independent India
The dominance of British rule without resistance
mcqs.explanation: Ex- The 1930s was a packed decade, considered the seed-time of modern independent India.

mcqs.question: Although normally resident in England, Mulk Raj Anand responded to events in India by:
options: Encouraging armed resistance against British rule
mcqs.explanation: Ex- For Anand, political action took the form of writing novels about the people and their struggles.

mcqs.question: Mulk Raj Anand's first five novels appeared in the following sequence:
options: Untouchable, Coolie, Two Leaves and a Bud, Across the Black Waters, The Village
Coolie, Untouchable, The Village, Two Leaves and a Bud, Across the Black Waters
The Village, Coolie, Untouchable, Two Leaves and a Bud, Across the Black Waters
Untouchable, Coolie, Two Leaves and a Bud, The Village, Across the Black Waters
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Anand's first five novels were published in the order: "Untouchable", "Coolie", "Two Leaves and a Bud", "The Village", and "Across the Black Waters".

mcqs.question: After the War, Mulk Raj Anand returned to India and settled in:
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Following the War, Anand returned to India and made Bombay his home.

mcqs.question: Mulk Raj Anand has been editing:
options: A journal on the arts called Marg
A newspaper for the Progressive Writers' Movement
A magazine on Indian history and culture
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Anand has been editing Marg, a high-class journal dedicated to the arts.

mcqs.question: Mulk Raj Anand's involvement in politics can be described as:
options: The primary focus of his life
A part, but not the whole, of his life
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Politics claimed a part, but not the whole, of Anand's life.

mcqs.question: Mulk Raj Anand's seven-volume work is:
options: A treatise on Hindu erotic art
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Anand's seven-volume work is an autobiographical novel.

mcqs.question: In his early novels, Mulk Raj Anand focused on:
options: The pariahs and the bottom dogs
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Anand ventured into territory largely ignored by Indian writers by writing about the pariahs and bottom dogs of society.

mcqs.question: Bankim Chandra's novels were:
options: Realistic depictions of the lower classes
Focused on the peasantry and humble folk
Naturalistic fiction in the style of Balzac or Zola
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Despite their nationalistic fervor, Bankim Chandra's novels were romances imitating Walter Scott.

mcqs.question: Tagore's novels primarily focused on:
options: The pariahs and the bottom dogs
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Tagore's interest lay chiefly in portraying the upper and middle classes in his novels.

mcqs.question: Sarat Chandra's novels dealt with:
options: The pariahs and the bottom dogs
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Sarat Chandra chose to write about the lower middle classes in his novels.

mcqs.question: Munshi Premchand's novels depicted:
options: The peasantry and humble folk of Uttar Pradesh
The upper and middle classes of Bengal
The pariahs and the bottom dogs of South India
The lower middle classes of Maharashtra
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Premchand's themes were drawn from the peasantry and humble folk of Uttar Pradesh.

mcqs.question: Mulk Raj Anand's aim was to show the West that the Orient had more than what was inferred from:
options: Omar Khayyam, Li Po, Tagore, and Kipling
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Anand wanted to demonstrate that the Orient had more to offer than the limited perspectives of Omar Khayyam, Li Po, Tagore, and Kipling.

mcqs.question: The central characters in Mulk Raj Anand's novels, such as Munoo, Bakha, and Gangu, were:
options: Representations of the elite and sophisticated
Depictions of the lower middle-class struggles
Symbolic of the exploited and marginalized
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Anand's protagonists, like Munoo, Bakha, and Gangu, were placed at the center of the scheme of cruelty and exploitation in India.

mcqs.question: Mulk Raj Anand's father, Lall Chand Anand, served in the:
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Anand's father served in the Indian Army, rising to the rank of Subedar.

mcqs.question: As a child, Mulk Raj Anand:
options: Mixed freely with children of sweepers
Had limited interaction with lower castes
Was discouraged from associating with other castes
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Anand mixed freely with the children of sweepers attached to his father's regiment, cutting across caste divisions.

mcqs.question: The heroes of Mulk Raj Anand's first novels were:
options: Reflections of real people he had known
Inspired by characters from Western literature
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Anand's heroes were dear to him because they were reflections of the real people he had known during his childhood and youth.

mcqs.question: Mulk Raj Anand viewed his writing as:
options: A way to gain fame and fortune
An artistic pursuit disconnected from reality
A way to repay the debt of gratitude to the people who inspired him
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Anand saw his writing as a way to repay the debt of gratitude he owed to the people who had inspired him to mature into manhood.

mcqs.question: When Mulk Raj Anand started writing fiction, he decided to:
options: Focus on the lives of the elite and sophisticated
Explore the bylanes of the outcastes and the peasants
Write romances in the style of Walter Scott
Imitate the naturalistic fiction of Balzac and Zola
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Anand chose to avoid the highways of romance and sophistication, instead exploring the lives of the outcastes, peasants, sepoys, and working people.

mcqs.question: For Mulk Raj Anand, writing about the proletariat was:
options: A laborious exercise of self-conscious proletarianism
The easier and more natural way
A means of gaining political favors
A way to appeal to Western audiences
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Writing about the proletariat was the easier and more natural way for Anand, as he considered himself one of them.

mcqs.question: The atmosphere of the late twenties and early thirties, as depicted in Mulk Raj Anand's novels, was:
options: Filled with political optimism and social harmony
Unaffected by the struggles of the common people
Dominated by the elite and the sophisticated
Filled with the dust of politics and the fumes of man's inhumanity to man
mcqs.explanation: Ex- The late 1920s and early 1930s, as portrayed in Anand's novels, were marked by political turmoil and social injustice, but not entirely devoid of hope.

mcqs.question: Before turning to political action through creative fiction, Mulk Raj Anand was a student of:
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Anand studied poetry, the Arts, and philosophy before using fiction for political action.

mcqs.question: Mulk Raj Anand's portrayal of the exploiter in his novels is often softened by:
options: A sense of the absurd and pity
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Anand's hatred for the exploiter was often tempered by a sense of the absurd and a feeling of pity.

mcqs.question: The novel "Two Leaves and a Bud" had to be withdrawn from circulation in England due to:
options: Threat of prosecution as an obscene book
mcqs.explanation: Ex- "Two Leaves and a Bud" faced a threat of prosecution for obscenity, leading to its withdrawal in England.

mcqs.question: During Mulk Raj Anand's visits to India, he was:
options: Pestered by the attentions of the C.I.D.
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Anand faced harassment from the C.I.D. during his visits to India.

mcqs.question: Mulk Raj Anand's novels were considered 'explosive' because:
options: The open expression of truth can be inciting and rebellious
They were poorly written and controversial
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Anand's novels were explosive as the open expression of truth can sometimes incite and rebel.

mcqs.question: Which of Mulk Raj Anand's novels is considered the most compact and artistically satisfying?
mcqs.explanation: Ex- "Untouchable" is regarded as Anand's most compact and artistically satisfying novel.

mcqs.question: The novel "Untouchable" covers the events of:
options: A single day in the life of Bakha
A week in the life of Bakha
A month in the life of Bakha
A year in the life of Bakha
mcqs.explanation: Ex- "Untouchable" depicts the events of a single day in the protagonist Bakha's life.

mcqs.question: Bakha, the protagonist of "Untouchable," is:
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Bakha is a low-caste sweeper, the son of Lakha, the Jemadar of sweepers in Bulashah.

mcqs.question: As a child of the twentieth century, Bakha:
options: Strictly adheres to traditional caste roles
Experiences stirrings due to new influences
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Being a 20th-century youth, Bakha feels stirrings within him caused by exposure to new influences.

mcqs.question: Despite the dirty nature of his job, Bakha:
options: Refuses to do his work properly
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Although Bakha's job is dirty, he manages to remain comparatively clean.

mcqs.question: Sohini, Bakha's sister, faces difficulty in:
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Sohini has to rely on the chance of a higher-caste person giving her water from the caste-well.

mcqs.question: The priest, Kali Nath, agrees to draw water for the outcastes:
options: As a cure for his constipation
Due to pressure from the community
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Kali Nath draws water for the outcastes more as a cure for his constipation than out of generosity.

mcqs.question: When Sohini goes to clean Kali Nath's courtyard, he:
options: Pays her fairly for her work
Refuses to let her enter his house
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Kali Nath makes improper suggestions to Sohini when she comes to clean his courtyard.

mcqs.question: Bakha's father, Lakha, tells the story of:
options: His own struggles as a sweeper
The Hakim Baghwan Das who cured Bakha
The importance of accepting one's caste
The need for a revolution against the caste system
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Lakha narrates the story of Hakim Baghwan Das, who once cured Bakha of a serious ailment.

mcqs.question: At the hockey game, Bakha:
options: Refuses to play with people of other castes
Scores a goal that starts a fight
mcqs.explanation: Ex- During the hockey match, Bakha scores a goal that triggers a free fight.

mcqs.question: When Bakha tries to help an injured boy, the boy's mother:
options: Accuses him of polluting the child
Asks him to take the boy to a doctor
mcqs.explanation: Ex- The injured boy's mother berates Bakha for 'polluting' her son by touching him.

mcqs.question: Colonel Hutchinson, the Salvationist, suggests that Bakha can end his caste by:
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Colonel Hutchinson advises Bakha to convert to Christianity to escape his caste.

mcqs.question: Mahatma Gandhi, in his public address, refers to untouchability as:
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Gandhi considers untouchability to be the greatest blot on Hinduism.

mcqs.question: According to Mahatma Gandhi, if he were to be born again, he would prefer to be born as:
options: A member of a higher caste
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Gandhi states that if reborn, he would choose to be born as an outcaste rather than in a higher caste.

mcqs.question: The poet Iqbal Nath Sarshar believes that the sweepers can be free from untouchability by:
options: Waiting for society to change its attitudes
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Iqbal Nath Sarshar suggests that sweepers can end their untouchable status by changing their profession.

mcqs.question: According to Iqbal Nath Sarshar, the introduction of a modern sanitary system like the flush will:
options: Make the sweepers' job more difficult
Eliminate the need for manual scavenging
Have no impact on the sweepers' status
mcqs.explanation: Ex- The poet believes that a modern flush system will free sweepers from manual scavenging.

mcqs.question: E. M. Forster, in his Foreword to "Untouchable," defends the epilogue by saying:
options: It is unnecessary and detracts from the story
It is the necessary climax that has mounted up with triple effect
It is a weak attempt at providing a solution
It is too optimistic and unrealistic
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Forster justifies the epilogue as a necessary climax that has built up with a triple effect.

mcqs.question: Bakha, as a character, is:
options: A typical representation of all untouchables
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Bakha is partly a prototypical untouchable and partly a unique individual.

mcqs.question: The events that happen to Bakha in the novel:
options: Could have happened and may still happen today
Were common occurrences in pre-independence India
mcqs.explanation: Ex- The incidents Bakha faces could have happened and might still occur in some places today.

mcqs.question: The dramatic telescoping of events in the novel is:
options: A flaw in the narrative structure
A technique used by Anand for effect
A result of poor planning and editing
An attempt to confuse the reader
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Anand deliberately telescopes numerous events into a short span for dramatic effect.

mcqs.question: The photographic fidelity of the novel convinces the reader due to:
options: The use of complex language and metaphors
The inclusion of historical facts and figures
The detailed descriptions of characters and settings
The author's personal experiences and observations
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Anand's personal experiences and observations lend the novel a convincing photographic fidelity.

mcqs.question: The novel "Untouchable" can be seen as:
options: A light-hearted story of a young boy's adventures
A critique of modernization and industrialization
An indictment of the evils of a decadent and perverted orthodoxy
A celebration of India's cultural heritage
mcqs.explanation: Ex- "Untouchable" serves as an indictment of the evils perpetuated by a decadent and perverted orthodoxy.

mcqs.question: The shifting scenes in the novel, from the temple to the market-place and the playground, are evoked with:
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Anand portrays the various scenes in the novel with an uncanny accuracy and attention to detail.

mcqs.question: As a novelist exposing social evils, Mulk Raj Anand is compared to:
mcqs.explanation: Ex- In his task of exposing societal evils, Anand is considered almost as effective as Charles Dickens.

mcqs.question: The picture of society presented in "Untouchable" is:
mcqs.explanation: Ex- The novel paints a picture of a place, society, and people that are not easily forgotten by the reader.

mcqs.question: Compared to "Untouchable," the novel "Coolie" is:
mcqs.explanation: Ex- "Coolie" is approximately twice the length of "Untouchable."

mcqs.question: According to Edwin Muir's classification, "Coolie" can be considered a:
mcqs.explanation: Ex- "Coolie" is what Edwin Muir would call a 'character' novel, as it extends primarily in space.

mcqs.question: The protagonist of "Coolie," Munoo, is a:
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Munoo, the hero of "Coolie," is a hill-boy.

mcqs.question: Munoo's journey in the novel takes him from:
options: Village to town, town to city, and city to Bombay and Simla
Bombay to Simla, Simla to village, and village to town
City to village, village to town, and town to Bombay
Simla to Bombay, Bombay to town, and town to village
mcqs.explanation: Ex- In "Coolie," Munoo's journey progresses from village to town, town to city, city to Bombay, and Bombay to Simla.

mcqs.question: While "Untouchable" can be considered a microcosm, "Coolie" is more like:
options: A focused study of a single character
A historical account of pre-independence India
A philosophical treatise on the human condition
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Compared to "Untouchable," "Coolie" is more like a macrocosm that represents Indian society.

mcqs.question: The general effect of "Coolie" can be described as:
options: Panoramic, with good and evil thrown together
Highly focused on a single theme
mcqs.explanation: Ex- "Coolie" has a panoramic effect, with good and evil being thrown together as in actual life.

mcqs.question: In "Coolie," the human situation:
options: Improves significantly as Munoo moves to different places
Remains largely the same wherever Munoo goes
Deteriorates rapidly as the novel progresses
Is not a central focus of the narrative
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Throughout "Coolie," the human situation hardly alters, regardless of where Munoo finds himself.

mcqs.question: The term 'coolie' has been used as:
options: A term of respect for manual laborers
A neutral descriptor for Indian workers
A term of derogation in India and elsewhere
A title reserved for highly skilled workers
mcqs.explanation: Ex- 'Coolie,' like 'untouchable,' has been and still is used as a term of derogation in India and other countries.

mcqs.question: Mulk Raj Anand's decision to humanize the 'coolie' in his novel was aimed at:
options: Reinforcing existing stereotypes about manual laborers
Providing a romanticized view of the working class
Giving the coolie feelings, a mind, a heart, and a soul
Criticizing the coolie's role in perpetuating social inequality
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Anand aimed to humanize the 'coolie' by giving him feelings, a mind, a heart, and a soul, thus raising his dignity as a human being.

mcqs.question: In "Coolie," Anand's indictment is primarily against:
options: The political system that enables inequality
Society as a whole for breeding prejudice, cupidity, and cruelty
The lack of education among the working class
mcqs.explanation: Ex- "Coolie" carries an indictment against society as a whole for breeding prejudice, cupidity, and cruelty.

mcqs.question: According to the novel, the root cause of the evil in society is:
mcqs.explanation: Ex- In "Coolie," poverty is identified as the root cause of the evil that infects society and renders it unsocial and inhuman.

mcqs.question: Munoo's life with his uncle and aunt in his village is:
mcqs.explanation: Ex- As an orphan, Munoo finds his life with his uncle and aunt in Bilasapur to be loveless enough.

mcqs.question: At Babu Nathoo Ram's house in Sham Nagar, Munoo finds:
options: A sort of madhouse where people are cruel
A haven from the hardships of his village life
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Munoo's experience at Babu Nathoo Ram's house in Sham Nagar proves to be like living in a madhouse, where people are cruel because they cannot be happy.

mcqs.question: The characters and developing action in the Cat Killers' Lane are described as having a:
mcqs.explanation: Ex- The characters and kaleidoscopic patterns of action in the Cat Killers' Lane have a Dickensian piquancy of realism.

mcqs.question: After his benefactor's bankruptcy, Munoo becomes:
options: A coolie in the grain market and a porter at the station
A student at a local school
An apprentice to a skilled craftsman
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Following his benefactor's bankruptcy, Munoo finds work as a coolie in the grain market and a porter at the station.

mcqs.question: Munoo is warned that the bigger a city is:
options: The more cruel it is to the sons of Adam
The easier it is to find success
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Before Munoo leaves for Bombay, he is warned that the bigger a city is, the more cruel it is to the sons of Adam.

mcqs.question: In Bombay, Munoo experiences all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Life on the pavements and in the slums
Service in the Sir George White Cotton Mills
Involvement in the 'labour trouble' and Hindu-Muslim disturbances
mcqs.explanation: Ex- While Munoo faces numerous hardships in Bombay, he does not find a stable and fulfilling career.

mcqs.question: Mrs. Mainwaring, the owner of the car that knocks down Munoo, is described as:
options: A woman of vast pretensions and no morals
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Mrs. Mainwaring is portrayed as a woman of vast pretensions and no morals.

mcqs.question: Munoo dies:
options: In Mrs. Mainwaring's house in Simla
Back in his village with his uncle and aunt
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Worn out by work as Mrs. Mainwaring's rickshaw-puller and page in Simla, Munoo hastens to his grave.

mcqs.question: The Spectator described Munoo as:
options: A stereotypical representation of the working class
mcqs.explanation: Ex- In its review of "Coolie," the Spectator referred to Munoo as a universal kind of figure.

mcqs.question: Munoo's attitude towards life can be described as:
options: A taste for the joy of life which is denied to him
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Munoo is characterized by his taste for the joy of life, which is repeatedly denied to him throughout the novel.

mcqs.question: Munoo's desires, as registered in his mind's eye, include:
options: A desire for revenge against his oppressors
A longing to escape his social class
Aspirations to become a wealthy businessman
Wanting to live, know, work, and grow up to be a strong man
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Munoo's desires, as described in the novel, include wanting to live, to know, to work, and to grow up to be a strong man.

mcqs.question: Munoo's character can be best described as:
options: Passive, with things happening to him
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Munoo is necessarily passive throughout the novel, with things just happening to him.

mcqs.question: Despite the hardships he faces, Munoo is:
options: A sensitive photographic plate that receives and preserves impressions
An unreliable narrator whose perceptions cannot be trusted
A detached observer who remains unaffected by his experiences
An active agent who shapes his own destiny
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Although passive, Munoo is likened to a sensitive photographic plate that accurately receives and preserves impressions.

mcqs.question: Munoo's positive qualities include all of the following EXCEPT:
mcqs.explanation: Ex- While Munoo possesses robust health, a thirst for life, and an unspoilt nature, he is not characterized by bitterness and resentment.

mcqs.question: Munoo and Bakha, the protagonist of "Untouchable," are described as:
options: Bitter rivals from different social classes
Unrelated characters with little in common
Symbols of the triumph of the human spirit
Heirs to the scalding frustration that is the birthright of millions
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Munoo and Bakha are portrayed as heirs to the scalding frustration that is the only birthright for millions born under the Indian sun.

mcqs.question: Anand's capacity to evoke diverse places, persons, moods, scenes, and situations is described as:
mcqs.explanation: Ex- The author's ability to evoke various elements in the novel is characterized as uncanny and unlaborious.

mcqs.question: The novel "Coolie" is considered:
options: A novel that excels in its sheer amplitude and power of narration
A niche work appealing to a limited audience
A departure from Anand's usual style and themes
mcqs.explanation: Ex- "Coolie" is regarded as a novel that excels in its sheer amplitude and power of narration, with few modern Indian novels surpassing it in this regard.

mcqs.question: The scenes in "Coolie" are described as:
options: Changing, with situations altering and colors jostling
mcqs.explanation: Ex- In "Coolie," the scenes change, situations alter, and colors jostle, creating a dynamic and varied narrative.

mcqs.question: The mixture of good and evil in "Coolie" is often:
options: Resolved in favor of good by the end of the novel
mcqs.explanation: Ex- In "Coolie," the interplay of good and evil is frequently covered by a dull grey, suggesting the complexity and ambiguity of life.

mcqs.question: If "Untouchable" has a piercing, lyrical quality and "Coolie" has an epic quality, "Two Leaves and a Bud" can be described as:
mcqs.explanation: Ex- "Two Leaves and a Bud" is considered essentially a 'dramatic' novel, culminating in a tragic clash of interests and destinies.

mcqs.question: The protagonist of "Two Leaves and a Bud," Gangu, travels from:
options: A village in North Western India to a tea estate in Assam
A village in South India to a factory in the North
Calcutta to a plantation in Ceylon
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Gangu crosses India horizontally from a village near Hoshiarpur in the Punjab to the Macpherson Tea Estate in Assam.

mcqs.question: Compared to Bakha and Munoo, Gangu is:
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Unlike the adolescent protagonists of the previous novels, Gangu is past middle age.

mcqs.question: The Tea Plantation in "Two Leaves and a Bud" is described as:
options: A world of freedom and opportunity
A world within a world, a prison apart
A place of harmony between the British and the Indians
A model of efficient industrial management
mcqs.explanation: Ex- The Tea Plantation is portrayed as a world within a world, a prison apart.

mcqs.question: The main pattern of tension in the novel is between:
options: The British managers and the Indian workers
The different ethnic groups among the coolies
The old and young generations of workers
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Superficially, the foreign exploiters and the masses of exploited coolies form the main pattern of tension in the novel.

mcqs.question: Dr. John de la Havre, a British character, is portrayed as:
options: A neutral observer of the plantation's affairs
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Dr. John de la Havre is one of the 'good', idealistic Britishers in the novel, whose consciousness is seeped with the agonizing memories of yesterday and the stinging woes of today.

mcqs.question: Dr. John de la Havre's love interest in the novel is:
options: A coolie woman on the plantation
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Dr. John de la Havre is in love with Barbara, the daughter of Croft-Cooke, the boss of the plantation.

mcqs.question: The villain of "Two Leaves and a Bud" is:
options: Croft-Cooke, the boss of the plantation
The Seth who buys cheap and sells dear to the coolies
mcqs.explanation: Ex- The villain of the novel is Reggie Hunt, the assistant manager, who is portrayed as sheer evil, compounded of cruelty and lust.

mcqs.question: Soon after his arrival at the plantation, Gangu realizes that:
options: He has found a land of opportunity
He has unwittingly walked into a trap
He will quickly rise through the ranks
He will be able to save enough money to return home
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Gangu soon realizes that he has unwittingly walked into a trap by coming to the tea plantation.

mcqs.question: Gangu's wife, Sajani, dies due to:
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Sajani dies after malaria breaks out on the plantation.

mcqs.question: The precarious 'peace' on the plantation is disrupted by:
options: A visit from a government official
A quarrel between two loose women
A strike organized by the coolies
mcqs.explanation: Ex- The fragile peace on the plantation is shattered when two loose women quarrel, leading to a violent incident involving Reggie.

mcqs.question: Dr. de la Havre's fate after the coolie demonstration is:
options: He is promoted to a higher position
He is killed by the plantation owners
He joins the coolies in their protest
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Due to his sympathies with the coolies, Dr. de la Havre is summarily dismissed after the demonstration.

mcqs.question: A tiger-shoot is staged on the plantation for:
options: The entertainment of the British managers
The greater glory of a visiting Governor
The amusement of the coolie children
mcqs.explanation: Ex- A tiger-shoot is stage-managed for the greater glory of a visiting Governor.

mcqs.question: In a mad accession of lust, Reggie approaches:
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Driven by lust and frustration, Reggie approaches Leila as she is plucking tea leaves alone.

mcqs.question: When Leila runs away from Reggie, he:
options: Lets her go and returns to his quarters
Chases her and apologizes for his behavior
Follows her to her house and shoots Gangu
Reports her to the plantation authorities
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Reggie follows Leila to her house, where he shoots blindly and kills Gangu.

mcqs.question: In the trial that follows Gangu's death, Mr. Justice Mowberley:
options: Finds Reggie guilty of culpable homicide
Finds Reggie not guilty and discharges him
Postpones the verdict due to lack of evidence
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Mr. Justice Mowberley, concurring with the majority view of the jury, finds Reggie 'not guilty' and discharges him.

mcqs.question: The title "Two Leaves and a Bud" is inspired by:
options: A quote from a famous novel
mcqs.explanation: Ex- The title "Two Leaves and a Bud" is inspired by the coolies' song about plucking tea leaves.

mcqs.question: The characterization in "Two Leaves and a Bud" is described as:
mcqs.explanation: Ex- The characterization in the novel is angular and sharp, with Reggie and de la Havre representing two extremes.

mcqs.question: One of the most memorable scenes in the novel is:
options: The coolie demonstration against the management
Leila's lone struggle with the python
Dr. de la Havre's dismissal from the plantation
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Leila's lone struggle with the python that has circled her in its deadly clasp is one of the unforgettable scenes in the novel.

mcqs.question: The novel "Two Leaves and a Bud" is influenced by:
mcqs.explanation: Ex- There are elements in "Two Leaves and a Bud" that suggest the influence of Forster's "A Passage to India," such as the atmosphere of suspicion, racial intolerance, and prejudice.

mcqs.question: Anand's writing in "Two Leaves and a Bud," particularly in portraying unpleasant characters, is:
mcqs.explanation: Ex- In portraying Reggie and other unpleasant characters, Anand's writing is infiltrated with disgust and hate.

mcqs.question: Anand compared his need to tell the unvarnished tale of plantation life to:
options: Leo Tolstoy's portrayal of Russian society
Charles Dickens' depiction of unsavoury aspects of Victorian life
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Anand felt compelled to tell the truth about plantation life in the 1930s, just as Dickens had to expose certain unsavoury aspects of Victorian life.

mcqs.question: In his next batch of three novels, Anand traces the career of:
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Anand's next trilogy of novels follows the career of Lalu Singh from boyhood to early manhood.

mcqs.question: The trilogy featuring Lalu Singh covers the period from:
options: Shortly before the First World War to the post-war era in India
The Indian Rebellion of 1857 to the end of the 19th century
The Partition of India to the early years of independence
The 1920s to the 1940s in Indian history
mcqs.explanation: Ex- The Lalu Singh trilogy spans the time from shortly before World War I to the disturbed post-war era in India, known as the Gandhian Age.

mcqs.question: Lalu Singh is first introduced as:
options: A young factory worker in Bombay
The youngest of a Sikh farmer's sons
An orphan living on the streets of Calcutta
A student at a British-run school
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Lalu Singh is initially portrayed as the youngest son of a Sikh farmer.

mcqs.question: The village of Nandpur, where Lalu Singh grows up, is:
options: A utopian community free from social ills
A microcosm of Indian village life, with its typical ingredients
An exceptionally progressive and modern village
A village wholly untouched by the influence of British colonialism
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Nandpur, in its main outlines, is like any other village in India, with the typical ingredients of village life.

mcqs.question: Lalu's act of rebellion in the neighbouring town involves:
options: Joining a political protest against British rule
Getting his hair cut at the King George Vth Haircutting and Shaving Saloon
mcqs.explanation: Ex- In a rebellious impulse, Lalu gets his kaishas (the visible insignia of Sikhism) shorn away at the King George Vth Haircutting and Shaving Saloon.

mcqs.question: Lalu's family reacts to his haircut by:
options: Feeling that he has disgraced the family
Accepting his decision as a sign of modernity
Encouraging him to further embrace Western culture
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Lalu's father feels that the family has been disgraced by his impious act of cutting his hair.

mcqs.question: Despite his love for his village, Lalu ultimately decides to:
options: Become a political activist to fight for change
Marry a local girl and settle down as a farmer
Enlist as a sepoy and leave the village
Continue his education in a nearby town
mcqs.explanation: Ex- The explosions of prejudice and hatred in the village make Lalu want to leave for good, and he enlists as a sepoy.

mcqs.question: Shortly before sailing from Karachi to fight in the war, Lalu learns that:
options: His brother has been arrested for murder
His village has been destroyed in a natural disaster
His family has disowned him for joining the army
mcqs.explanation: Ex- Before leaving for the war, Lalu hears that his father has passed away, but his new-found friends in the army help him bear the shock.

mcqs.question: What is the title of the second novel in the Lalu trilogy?
mcqs.explanation: Ex- The passage mentions that in the second novel of the Lalu trilogy, Lalu's experiences in France are detailed.

content.value: # R.K. Narayan

R.K. Narayan, born in 1907 in Madras (now Chennai), stands as one of India’s most celebrated and influential authors of the 20th century. Writing primarily in English, Narayan carved out a unique space in Indian literature, creating a bridge between the East and the West through his simple yet profound storytelling. His works, mostly set in the fictional town of Malgudi, offer a window into the complexities of Indian society, human nature, and the universal experiences that bind us all.
Early Life and Career

Narayan’s mother tongue was Tamil, but he chose to write in English, a decision that would shape his career and contribute to the development of Indian literature in English. He settled in Mysore, which would become the inspiration for his fictional town of Malgudi.

His first novel, “Swami and Friends,” published in 1935, marked the birth of Malgudi and set the tone for much of his future work. This novel, along with “The Bachelor of Arts” (1936) and “The English Teacher” (1945), form what is often considered a trilogy, offering a comprehensive view of life in Malgudi.
The Malgudi Universe
Creation and Evolution of Malgudi

Malgudi, Narayan’s fictional town, is more than just a setting; it’s a character in itself, evolving and changing throughout his novels. Located on the banks of the river Sarayu, Malgudi serves as a microcosm of India, reflecting the country’s social, cultural, and economic changes over time.

In his early novels, Malgudi is portrayed as a placid, almost idyllic town. However, as Narayan’s career progresses, Malgudi faces “irresistible external pressures,” losing some of its former innocence. This evolution mirrors the changes in Indian society, particularly in the post-independence era.
Landmarks and Geography

Malgudi is vividly brought to life through its landmarks and geography. The Sarayu River, a constant presence, symbolizes the flow of life and the inevitability of change. The Market Road is described as the “life-line of Malgudi” in “Mr. Sampath.” Other notable locations include Lawley Extension (later renamed Gandhi Nagar), the Mempi Hills, and Nallappa’s Mango Grove.

The expansion of Malgudi is hinted at in later novels, with mentions of a new bridge across the Sarayu, in addition to the existing railway bridge. This growth reflects the development and modernization of India itself.
Major Themes and Narrative Techniques
The Absurdity of Existence

One of the central themes in Narayan’s work, particularly in his later novels, is the absurdity of existence. He portrays the world as a field of unpredictable and uncontrollable forces, a theatre where farces and tragi-comedies play out endlessly. This philosophical vision is often conveyed through “exquisite patterns of folly and self-deception” in his characters.
The Interplay of Tradition and Modernity

Narayan’s novels often explore the tension between traditional Indian values and the encroaching forces of modernization. However, he neither intolerantly criticizes Indian ways nor fanatically defends them, presenting instead a balanced view of both tradition and modernity.
The Cycle of Disturbance and Restoration

A typical pattern in Narayan’s novels involves a disturbance of the established order, followed by a return to normalcy. This cycle often manifests as a flight, an uprooting, or a disruption, followed by a return, renewal, or restoration. This pattern reflects Narayan’s belief in the resilience of life and the human spirit.
Narrative Technique

Narayan’s narrative style is characterized by its simplicity and directness. In novels like “The Guide,” he employs a non-linear narrative structure, jumping between past and present, which adds depth and complexity to the story without confusing the reader.
Major Works and Characters
Swami and Friends (1935)

This novel introduces the character of Swami, a schoolboy whose adventures and misadventures form the core of the story. Swami’s friends, including the self-important Somu, the “mighty good-for-nothing” Mani, Samuel (known as “Pea”), and the dashing Rajam, create a vivid picture of childhood in colonial India.
The Bachelor of Arts (1936)
This novel continues the coming-of-age theme, focusing on a young man’s journey through college and into adulthood.
The English Teacher (1945)

Considered one of Narayan’s most moving works, “The English Teacher” tells the story of Krishna, an English teacher, and his wife Susila. The novel explores themes of love, loss, and spiritual awakening. The portrayal of Krishna and Susila’s blissful married life and Krishna’s anguish during Susila’s illness is considered one of the most poignant parts of Narayan’s oeuvre.
The Financial Expert (1952)

This novel follows the rise and fall of Margayya, a financial advisor whose obsession with money leads him through a series of adventures and misadventures. Margayya’s character development is traced through five phases: peasants’ advisor, publisher, money-lender, financial wizard, and finally, insolvent.
The Guide (1958)

Often considered Narayan’s masterpiece, “The Guide” tells the story of Raju, a tourist guide who becomes entangled in the lives of Rosie and her husband Marco. The novel employs a non-linear narrative, jumping between Raju’s past and present, creating suspense and anticipation. The character of Rosie stands out as one of Narayan’s strongest female characters, pursuing her ambition to become a dancer.
The Man-Eater of Malgudi (1961)

This novel portrays a conflict between the well-meaning printer Nataraj and the bullying taxidermist Vasu, symbolizing the battle between good and evil. The Mempi hills play a significant role in this novel, representing the untamed forces of nature.
The Sweet-Vendor (1967)

The novel centers around Jagan, a sweet-vendor, and his son Mali. It explores themes of generational conflict and the tension between tradition and modernity. Mali’s ambition to manufacture novel-writing machines contrasts sharply with Jagan’s traditional sweet-making business.
Character Portrayals

Narayan’s characters are often described as “diminished Don Quixotes and their Dulcinea del Tobosos,” highlighting their quixotic and sometimes delusional nature. His protagonists are typically ordinary individuals caught up in extraordinary circumstances, rather than powerful or influential figures.

Female characters in Narayan’s novels often play significant roles. While some, like Susila in “The English Teacher,” embody traditional values, others, like Rosie in “The Guide,” break the mold and pursue their own ambitions.
Style and Language

Narayan’s greatest strength as a writer is his masterful command of the English language. He writes with simplicity and directness, avoiding elaborate or flowery prose. This straightforward style allows him to convey subtle shades of feeling and thought effectively.

Unlike some of his contemporaries, such as Mulk Raj Anand, Narayan rarely uses swear words or explicit content in his writing. His style is more understated and subtle, focusing on the everyday experiences and inner lives of his characters.
Humor and Irony

Humor plays a crucial role in Narayan’s writing. He often employs a gentle, ironic humor that helps balance the serious themes in his novels. This humor serves to highlight the absurdities of life and human behavior without resorting to harsh satire or cynicism.
Religion and Spirituality

Religion and spirituality are integral parts of the world Narayan creates. He portrays religion as deeply ingrained in Indian society, influencing the daily lives and decisions of his characters. However, his treatment of faith is often ambiguous, especially in his later novels. Faith is often “arrested at the brink,” leaving characters and readers in a state of uncertainty.
Criticism and Legacy

While Narayan’s work has been widely praised, some critics have pointed out certain limitations. His later novels have been criticized for relying too heavily on “hackneyed Indian motifs” like cobras, Bharatanatyam, and bogus Sadhus. Some characters, particularly in novels like “The Financial Expert,” have been described as caricatures rather than fully developed individuals.

Despite these criticisms, Narayan’s contribution to Indian literature in English is immense. His ability to create a vivid, believable world in Malgudi, his insightful portrayal of human nature, and his exploration of universal themes have earned him a place among the greatest Indian writers of the 20th century.
Conclusion

R.K. Narayan’s body of work offers a unique and invaluable perspective on Indian life and universal human experiences. Through his fictional town of Malgudi and its inhabitants, Narayan explores the complexities of human relationships, the tension between tradition and modernity, and the often absurd nature of existence itself.

His simple yet profound style, his gentle humor, and his deep understanding of human nature have made his works accessible and relevant to readers across cultures and generations. While rooted in the specific context of mid-20th century India, Narayan’s novels transcend their setting to offer insights into the human condition that remain relevant today.

As we look back on Narayan’s legacy, we see a writer who managed to capture the essence of Indian life while speaking to universal human experiences. His works continue to be read, studied, and appreciated, cementing his place as one of the most important Indian authors of the 20th century.

Q29: What is suggested as the real 'hero' of Narayan's novels and stories?
A) The main characters
B) Malgudi itself
C) The Sarayu river
D) The Mempi Hills
Answer: B
Ex- The passage proposes the interesting theory that the fictional town of Malgudi is the real 'hero' of Narayan's works, with its enduring soul.
Q30: Which line from a poem is used to describe the timeless essence of Malgudi?
A) "Things fall apart; the centre cannot hold"
B) "Gather ye rosebuds while ye may"
C) "The One remains, the Many change and pass"
D) "Time present and time past are both perhaps present in time future"
Answer: C
Ex- The line "The One remains, the Many change and pass" is quoted to capture how the essence of Malgudi remains the same despite the changes over time.
Q1: According to the passage, what do Narayan's characters seem to achieve?
A) Fame and fortune
B) A sort of transmigration from body to body
C) Complete transformation of personality
D) Resolution of all conflicts
Answer: B
Ex- on closer scrutiny, Narayan's characters seem to transmigrate from one body and name to another.
Q2: Who is described as "also the Bachelor of Arts" and "presently Krishnan the English Teacher"?
A) Ramani
B) Mr. Sampath
C) Swami
D) Rajam
Answer: C
Ex- Swami, the schoolboy character, is linked to the protagonists of Bachelor of Arts and The English Teacher.
Q3: Which character is described as an "agreeable rascal"?
A) Swami
B) Mr. Sampath
C) Margayya
D) Vasu
Answer: B
Ex- Mr. Sampath is characterized as an agreeable rascal who shares qualities with Margayya, Raju, Vasu and Mali.
Q4: In Narayan's novels, how is human nature presented?
A) With overt condemnation or praise
B) As purely good or evil
C) Veraciously and interestingly
D) As constantly changing and unpredictable
Answer: C
Ex- The passage states that human nature is presented veraciously, interestingly and memorably in Narayan's novels, without overt judgment.
Q5: What is described as the one theme of Narayan's fictional works?
A) The struggle between good and evil
B) The search for meaning in life
C) Malgudi and Malgudi humanity
D) The conflict between tradition and modernity
Answer: C
Ex- Malgudi and the humanity inhabiting it are proposed as the unifying theme across Narayan's various novels and stories.
Q6: Who imaginatively reviews the possible history of Malgudi since Puranic times?
A) Swami
B) Srinivas the scenario-writer
C) The Bachelor of Arts
D) Margayya the financial expert
Answer: B
Ex- In Mr. Sampath, the character Srinivas the scenario-writer imaginatively passes in review the mythical and historical events that may have taken place in Malgudi.
Q7: Which novel is described as the most enjoyable in some respects?
A) The Guide
B) The English Teacher
C) The Financial Expert
D) Swami and Friends
Answer: D
Ex- The passage suggests that Swami and Friends is in some ways the most enjoyable of Narayan's novels.
Q8: Who are some of Swami's friends mentioned in the text?
A) Somu, Mani, Samuel and Rajam
B) Krishna, Susila and Leela
C) Ramani, Savitri and Shanta
D) Margayya, Balu and Brinda
Answer: A
Ex- Swami's friends described in the novel include the self-important Somu, the "mighty good-for-nothing" Mani, Samuel known as "Pea", and the dashing Rajam.
Q9: Under which teachers is Swami mentioned to have studied?
A) Vedanayakam and Ebenezar
B) Samuel and Krishna
C) Srinivas and Margayya
D) Marco and Rosie
Answer: A
Ex- Swami is said to have studied under the "fire-eyed" Vedanayakam and the fanatical Ebenezar.
Q10: In the story "Father's Help", what does Swami lie to his father about?
A) His friend Rajam
B) His teacher Samuel
C) His progress in school
D) His involvement in a cricket match
Answer: B
Ex- In the short story, Swami initially lies to his father about Samuel, the geography teacher.
Q11: What does Swami eagerly wish for after his father writes a complaint to the headmaster?
A) To be praised by Samuel
B) To be made the class monitor
C) To be caned by Samuel
D) To be excused from homework
Answer: C
Ex- After his lies lead to his father complaining, Swami wishes to be caned by Samuel so that his earlier statements may be justified.
Q12: How does the text describe Swami and Friends, Bachelor of Arts, and The English Teacher?
A) As a trilogy of Malgudi-on-Sarayu
B) As unrelated works with different themes
C) As political allegories of Indian independence
D) As part of a series featuring the same characters
Answer: A
Ex- The three novels are practically considered a trilogy set in the fictional town of Malgudi on the banks of the Sarayu river.
Q13: In contrast to The English Teacher, how is The Dark Room characterized?
A) As a story of marital harmony
B) As a fantasy novel
C) As a study of domestic disharmony
D) As a detective mystery
Answer: C
Ex- While The English Teacher depicts marital love, The Dark Room is described as a study of domestic disharmony.
Q14: What is a significant difference between Ramani and Krishna?
A) Their occupation
B) Their marital status
C) Their place of residence
D) Their children's names
Answer: A
Ex- Ramani is an insurance executive, whereas Krishna is a teacher of English poetry, which is noted as a significant difference between them.
Q15: How is Savitri compared to Susila?
A) As equally poetic and eternally feminine
B) As having a greater capacity for forgiveness
C) As lacking Susila's ineluctable poetry and femininity
D) As more assertive of her rights as a woman
Answer: C
Ex- Savitri is said to lack the poetry and blend of divine and human womanhood that characterize Susila.
Q16: What disrupts Ramani and Savitri's relatively happy married life?
A) Ramani's job loss
B) Savitri's illness
C) The arrival of Shanta, Ramani's love interest
D) The coupl\<eos financial troubles
Answer: C
Ex- The entrance of the glamorous Shanta, with whom Ramani becomes infatuated, disrupts his domestic life with Savitri.
Q17: To which literary character is Savitri compared when she asserts her rights?
A) Ophelia from Hamlet
B) Desdemona from Othello
C) Nora from A Doll's House
D) Portia from The Merchant of Venice
Answer: C
Ex- When Savitri leaves Ramani asserting her autonomy as a woman, she is compared to Nora from Ibsen's play A Doll's House.
Q18: What metaphorical phrase is used to refer to Savitri's marital home?
A) The dark room
B) The doll's house
C) The gilded cage
D) The prison cell
Answer: B
Ex- Savitri is described as defiantly walking out of the "doll's house", drawing a parallel to Ibsen's play.
Q19: Who rescues Savitri when she is about to be carried away by the river?
A) Ramani
B) A burglar
C) Shanta
D) Her children
Answer: B
Ex- After leaving home, Savitri is rescued by a burglar when she is on the verge of being swept away by the river.
Q20: What does Ramani do while Savitri is away from home?
A) Searches frantically for her
B) Files a missing person report with the police
C) Leaves the children in a cinema and meets Shanta
D) Reconciles with Savitri's parents
Answer: C
Ex- In Savitri's absence, Ramani leaves the children at the cinema for a couple of hours while he spends time with Shanta.
Q21: What prompts Savitri to return home despite her earlier defiance?
A) Concern for her children
B) Realization of her financial dependence
C) Pressure from her own parents
D) Ramani's pleas for forgiveness
Answer: A
Ex- Though initially determined, Savitri decides to return home as she keeps thinking about her children.
Q22: How does the narrator describe the ending of The Dark Room?
A) As a happy reconciliation
B) As a tragedy
C) As a cynical conclusion
D) As an unexpected twist
Answer: C
Ex- The narrator calls the ending, where Savitri returns and Ramani's affair continues, a "cynical conclusion".
Q23: Which ancient Tamil story are Ramani and Savitri compared to?
A) Kovalan and Kannaki
B) Rama and Sita
C) Shiva and Parvati
D) Krishna and Radha
Answer: A
Ex- Ramani and Savitri's story is likened to the ancient Tamil tale of Kovalan and Kannaki.
Q24: In The English Teacher, how is the accidental meeting between Krishna and Susila at the railway station described?
A) As a tense and awkward encounter
B) As a moment of subdued ecstasy
C) As a purely business-like interaction
D) As an angry confrontation
Answer: B
Ex- Krishna's reunion with his wife and child on the railway platform is portrayed as a moment of understated joy and romance.
Q25: What does Krishna pray for at the temple during his outing with Susila?
A) For a child
B) For a new house
C) For a job promotion
D) For Susila's wellbeing
Answer: D
Ex- Moved by the glow on Susila's face in the temple, Krishna prays "God bless this child and protect her".
Q26: What illness does Susila contract, leading to her untimely death?
A) Cholera
B) Malaria
C) Typhoid
D) Tuberculosis
Answer: C
Ex- Susila falls ill with typhoid, which proves fatal despite Krishna's desperate hoping.
Q27: How does Narayan's description of Susila's illness and death affect the reader?
A) It leaves the reader unmoved
B) It is overly sentimental and cloying
C) It is one of the most moving pieces of writing
D) It is clinical and detached
Answer: C
Ex- The account of Krishna and Susila's blissful married life and his anguish during her illness is considered one of the most moving and flawless parts of the novel.
Q28: What element is introduced in the second half of The English Teacher that contrasts with the realism of the first half?
A) Time travel
B) Ghostly hauntings
C) Psychic communication with the dead
D) An alternate reality
Answer: C
Ex- Krishna's attempts to communicate psychically with the deceased Susila, with the help of a medium, bring a whimsical or fantastical element to the novel.
Q29: At the end of the novel, how does Susila return to Krishna?
A) Through a dream
B) By a miracle
C) As a ghost
D) In his imagination
Answer: B
Ex- In the last scene, Susila miraculously returns to Krishna's side, more radiant than ever, in what he calls a "moment of rare, immutable joy".
Q30: How does Krishna describe the moment of reuniting with Susila at the end?
A) As a trick of the mind
B) As a moment of despair
C) As a moment for which one feels grateful to Life and Death
D) As an impossible fantasy
Answer: C
Ex- Krishna says the profound moment where his and Susila's personalities dissolve and merge is one "for which one feels grateful to Life and Death".
Q1: In which novel does R. K. Narayan's protagonist venture out of Malgudi?
A) The Financial Expert
B) The Guide
C) Waiting for the Mahatma
D) The Sweet-Vendor
Answer: C
Ex- Waiting for the Mahatma is exceptional as the action strays out of Malgudi, going as far as Delhi.
Q2: What is the central theme of Waiting for the Mahatma?
A) Terrorism
B) Gandhian politics
C) Bharati-Sriram romance
D) Life in Malgudi
Answer: C
Ex- The theme is apparently the Bharati-Sriram romance which gains a new dimension with their common allegiance to Gandhi.
Q3: How does the author feel about Narayan's art in Waiting for the Mahatma?
A) It betrays unsureness and perplexity
B) It is his best work
C) It perfectly resolves the duality of interest
D) It is a mediocre effort
Answer: A
Ex- Denied the security of Malgudi and dealing with Gandhian politics, Narayan's art betrays unsureness and perplexity.
Q4: What change does the author observe in Malgudi in Narayan's later novels?
A) Malgudi remains unchanged
B) Malgudi becomes more traditional
C) Malgudi loses its innocence and faces external pressures
D) Malgudi completely transforms into a modern city
Answer: C
Ex- The placid Malgudi of earlier novels gives way to a town facing irresistible external pressures, losing its former innocence.
Q5: What is Srinivas-Narayan's 'Pisgah-Vision' of existence?
A) Existence as a harmonious balance
B) Existence as a journey towards perfection
C) Existence as Folly and Absurdity
D) Existence as a battlefield between good and evil
Answer: C
Ex- Srinivas-Narayan sees all existence as Folly and Absurdity, with things balancing themselves in infinite concentric circles.
Q6: How does the author describe the characters in Mr. Sampath?
A) Realistic and relatable
B) Dickensian or Wodehousian
C) Flat and underdeveloped
D) Complex and psychologically deep
Answer: B
Ex- The author describes quite a few characters in Mr. Sampath as Dickensian or Wodehousian, implying they are eccentric and humorous.
Q7: What is the climactic scene in the shooting of The Burning of Kama?
A) Shiva and Parvathi's embrace
B) Ravi rushing between Shiva and Parvathi
C) The dance performance
D) The final shot of the film
Answer: B
Ex- The climax occurs when mad Ravi rushes between Shiva and Parvathi, hurls the god down, and carries Parvathi away, ruining the picture.
Q8: What happens to Sampath at the end of the novel?
A) He marries Shanti
B) He returns to his old life
C) His whereabouts are unknown
D) He walks forlornly towards the railway station
Answer: D
Ex- In the last scene, Sampath informs Srinivas that Shanti has left him and is seen walking rather forlornly towards the railway station.
Q9: How does the author view the main characters in The Financial Expert?
A) Well-developed and realistic
B) Caricatures
C) Inspiring and heroic
D) Forgettable and bland
Answer: B
Ex- The author considers the main defect of the novel to be that the chief characters are little better than caricatures.
Q10: What are the five phases of Margayya's development in the novel?
A) Peasant, publisher, money-lender, wizard, insolvent
B) Advisor, printer, banker, depositor, publisher
C) Banker, publisher, investor, millionaire, pauper
D) Farmer, businessman, politician, financial expert, bankrupt
Answer: A
Ex- Margayya's development is traced through five phases: peasants' advisor, publisher, money-lender, financial wizard, and finally insolvent.
Q11: What is the relationship between Dr. Pal and Margayya?
A) They are business partners
B) Dr. Pal is Margayya's mentor
C) They are apostles of sex and money respectively
D) They are rivals in business
Answer: C
Ex- Dr. Pal and Margayya are described as the apostles of sex and money respectively, hinting at a chain of nemesis in their intersecting relationships.
Q12: What does Margayya consider the greatest wonder of creation?
A) Love
B) Nature
C) Interest on money
D) Human relationships
Answer: C
Ex- For Margayya, interest on money is the greatest wonder of creation, combining the mystery of birth and multiplication, bordering on mystic perception.
Q13: How does the author characterize Margayya's obsession with money?
A) A practical necessity
B) A means to help others
C) A mystic perception
D) A dangerous addiction
Answer: C
Ex- Margayya's obsession with money and the system of compounding interest is described as a mystic perception, reflecting endlessly like opposite mirrors.
Q14: What ultimately happens to the money invested in Margayya's bank?
A) It is safely returned to investors
B) It is donated to charity
C) It is lost forever
D) It is used to expand the business
Answer: C
Ex- The money invested by racketeers and profiteers in Margayya's bank is ultimately lost forever down the drain of his vast speculation.
Q15: How does the author view The Financial Expert as a piece of writing?
A) Dull and preachy
B) Entertaining and enlightening
C) Overly complex and confusing
D) Superficial and forgettable
Answer: B
Ex- The author considers The Financial Expert a capital piece of writing, as entertaining as it is enlightening, on shady business values and the worship of money.
Q16: What is the central focus of Narayan's later novels, as per the passage?
A) Gandhian politics
B) Rural life in Malgudi
C) Exotic characters and their eccentricities
D) Philosophical musings on life
Answer: C
Ex- Narayan's later novels, beginning with Mr. Sampath, focus on an exotic world of half-hearted dreamers, adventurers, eccentrics, and cranks.
Q17: How does the author describe the tone of The Financial Expert?
A) Heavily satirical
B) Mildly satirical
C) Completely serious
D) Overtly moralistic
Answer: B
Ex- The Financial Expert is described as clearly written, mildly satirical, and unexcitingly interesting and entertaining.
Q18: What role does Mrs. Margayya play in the novel?
A) She opposes Margayya's schemes
B) She is a link between Margayya and Balu
C) She is a silent observer
D) She encourages Margayya's risky investments
Answer: B
Ex- Mrs. Margayya serves as a link between the careers of father and son, putting up with everything and trying to smooth things over.
Q19: How does Balu's character develop over the course of the novel?
A) From a spoilt child to a responsible adult
B) From a studious boy to a wastrel and finally a sobered man
C) He remains unchanged throughout
D) From a rebellious youth to a successful businessman
Answer: B
Ex- Balu's character arc takes him from a reluctant schoolboy to a failed student, a wastrel and rake, and finally a sobered man returning to his roots.
Q20: What is Dr. Pal's role in Margayya's downfall?
A) He embezzles money from Margayya's bank
B) He spreads rumors about Margayya's insolvency
C) He encourages depositors to withdraw their money
D) He brings down Margayya's financial house of cards
Answer: D
Ex- Dr. Pal proves to be Balu's evil genius and ultimately brings down Margayya's financial house of cards to the ground.
Q21: What is the significance of Malgudi in Narayan's earlier novels?
A) It is merely a backdrop for the stories
B) It is a character in itself
C) It represents urban India
D) It is an imaginary town with no real significance
Answer: B
Ex- In Narayan's first three or four novels, Malgudi itself was like a character, but in later novels, it becomes merely a location for the stories.
Q22: How does Narayan view the world in his later novels?
A) As a harmonious and perfect place
B) As a field of unpredictable and uncontrollable forces
C) As a place where goodness and beauty thrive
D) As a static and unchanging environment
Answer: B
Ex- In his later novels, Narayan sees the world as a field of unpredictable and uncontrollable forces, a theatre where farces and tragi-comedies play out endlessly.
Q23: What is the author's opinion on the presence of sheer goodness or beauty in Narayan's world?
A) They are abundant and easily found
B) They are present in a pure and unadulterated form
C) They are rare and must appear mixed with tawdriness and stupidity
D) They are completely absent
Answer: C
Ex- The author believes that in Narayan's world, there is little room for sheer goodness or beauty; if present, they must appear mixed with tawdriness, stupidity, and cupidity.
Q24: How does the author compare Narayan's later novels to his earlier ones?
A) The later novels are more intense and focused
B) The later novels are more expansive and varied
C) There is no significant difference between the two
D) The later novels are more philosophically profound
Answer: B
Ex- While Narayan's later novels gain in extension and variety compared to his earlier works, they lose in terms of intensity.
Q25: What is the central theme of Narayan's novel The Guide?
A) Gandhian politics
B) Romance and relationships
C) The role of religion in society
D) The theme is not mentioned in the passage
Answer: D
Ex- While The Guide is mentioned as one of Narayan's later novels, the passage does not elaborate on its central theme.
Q26: How does the passage characterize the post-war years in Narayan's novels?
A) As a time of stability and certainty
B) As a period of hectic striving and chronic uncertainty
C) As a return to traditional values
D) As a time of peace and prosperity
Answer: B
Ex- The post-war years in Narayan's novels are described as a time of hectic striving, chronic uncertainty, expense of spirit, and lust in action.
Q27: What is the author's view on Narayan's portrayal of the absurdity of existence?
A) It is unconvincing and poorly executed
B) It is the central message of his novels
C) It is captured through exquisite patterns of folly and self-deception
D) It is a minor theme overshadowed by other concerns
Answer: C
Ex- The author believes Narayan's later novels capture the absurdity of existence through exquisite patterns of folly and self-deception.
Q28: How does the author describe the characters in Narayan's later novels?
A) As realistic and relatable figures
B) As mythological archetypes
C) As mouthpieces for Narayan's philosophy
D) As diminished Don Quixotes and their Dulcinea del Tobosos
Answer: D
Ex- The characters in Narayan's later novels are described as diminished Don Quixotes and their Dulcinea del Tobosos, highlighting their quixotic and delusional nature.
Q29: What is the significance of the Sarayu river in the changing landscape of Malgudi?
A) It remains a constant presence amidst the changes
B) It is a symbol of the town's resistance to modernity
C) It is spanned by a new bridge, indicating Malgudi's growth
D) It is not mentioned in the passage
Answer: C
Ex- The passage mentions that there is talk of a new bridge across the Sarayu, in addition to the existing railway bridge, signifying Malgudi's expansion and development.
Q30: How does the author view Narayan's philosophical vision in his later novels?
A) As a celebration of the triumph of the human spirit
B) As a bleak and pessimistic outlook on life
C) As a balanced and realistic portrayal of existence
D) As a comical and farcical representation of the world
Answer: D
Ex- Narayan's philosophical vision in his later novels is described as a comical and absurd representation of the world, where farces and tragi-comedies play out endlessly.
Q1: Who is the protagonist of Narayan's novel The Guide?
A) Marco
B) Rosie
C) Velan
D) Raju
Answer: D
Ex- Raju is the principal character in The Guide, playing many roles and putting into practice ideas on tourism.
Q2: What is Raju's character compared to in the novel?
A) A romantic hero
B) A tragic figure
C) A romantic doubled with a rascal
D) A spiritual guide
Answer: C
Ex- Raju is described as a romantic doubled with a rascal, similar to Narayan's previous protagonists like Margayya and Sampath.
Q3: What happens to Raju at the end of the novel?
A) He becomes a successful tourist guide
B) He marries Rosie
C) He undertakes a fast and possibly dies
D) He returns to his old life
Answer: C
